claim: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing has yet to be reported in species of the Platyhelminthes.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing has yet to be reported in species of the Platyhelminthes.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field at the time of publication, representing established knowledge about what has been reported in the literature.

claim: Omega-1 is a secreted ribonuclease crucial for Th2 polarization and granuloma formation.
source: This secreted ribonuclease is crucial for Th2 polarization and granuloma formation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the field, as indicated in the introduction and discussion sections.

claim: Schistosome eggs were exposed to Cas9 complexed with guide RNA complementary to ω1 by electroporation.
source: Schistosome eggs were exposed to Cas9 complexed with guide RNA complementary to ω1 by electroporation or by transduction with lentiviral particles.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Schistosome eggs were exposed to Cas9 complexed with guide RNA complementary to ω1 by transduction with lentiviral particles.
source: Schistosome eggs were exposed to Cas9 complexed with guide RNA complementary to ω1 by electroporation or by transduction with lentiviral particles.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Some eggs were transfected with a single stranded donor template.
source: Some eggs were also transfected with a single stranded donor template.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Sequences of amplicons from gene-edited parasites exhibited Cas9-catalyzed mutations including homology directed repaired alleles.
source: Sequences of amplicons from gene-edited parasites exhibited Cas9-catalyzed mutations including homology directed repaired alleles, and other analyses revealed depletion of ω1 transcripts and the ribonuclease.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including sequencing results.

claim: Gene-edited parasites showed depletion of ω1 transcripts.
source: Sequences of amplicons from gene-edited parasites exhibited Cas9-catalyzed mutations including homology directed repaired alleles, and other analyses revealed depletion of ω1 transcripts and the ribonuclease.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including transcript analysis.

claim: Gene-edited parasites showed depletion of the ω1 ribonuclease.
source: Sequences of amplicons from gene-edited parasites exhibited Cas9-catalyzed mutations including homology directed repaired alleles, and other analyses revealed depletion of ω1 transcripts and the ribonuclease.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including ribonuclease activity assays.

claim: Gene-edited eggs failed to polarize Th2 cytokine responses in macrophage/T-cell co-cultures.
source: Gene-edited eggs failed to polarize Th2 cytokine responses in macrophage/T-cell co-cultures, while the volume of pulmonary granulomas surrounding ω1-mutated eggs following tail-vein injection into mice was vastly reduced.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from co-culture experiments.

claim: The volume of pulmonary granulomas surrounding ω1-mutated eggs following tail-vein injection into mice was vastly reduced.
source: Gene-edited eggs failed to polarize Th2 cytokine responses in macrophage/T-cell co-cultures, while the volume of pulmonary granulomas surrounding ω1-mutated eggs following tail-vein injection into mice was vastly reduced.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from in vivo mouse experiments.

claim: Schistosomiasis is considered the most virulent of the human helminth diseases in terms of morbidity and mortality.
source: Schistosomiasis is considered the most virulent of the human helminth diseases in terms of morbidity and mortality (Gryseels et al., 2006; Hotez, 2014a; Hotez, 2014b; Hotez et al., 2008; Colley, 2014; Colley et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The past decade has seen major advances in knowledge and understanding of the pathophysiology, developmental biology, evolutionary relationships and genome annotation of the human schistosomes.
source: The past decade has seen major advances in knowledge and understanding of the pathophysiology, developmental biology, evolutionary relationships and genome annotation of the human schistosomes (Berriman et al., 2009; Young et al., 2012; Lepesant et al., 2011; Geyer et al., 2011; Vanderstraete et al., 2014; Rinaldi et al., 2012a; Rinaldi et al., 2012b; Protasio et al., 2012; Valentim et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013; Collins et al., 2013; Hagen et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Establishing CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing in schistosomiasis would greatly enable effective functional genomics approaches.
source: Establishing CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing in schistosomiasis would greatly enable effective functional genomics approaches.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the technology.

claim: Stable CRISPR/Cas9-based site-specific gene mutation and phenotyping will drive innovation and a deeper understanding of schistosome pathogenesis, biology and evolution.
source: Stable CRISPR/Cas9-based site-specific gene mutation and phenotyping will drive innovation and a deeper understanding of schistosome pathogenesis, biology and evolution (Hoffmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the technology, supported by a citation.

claim: The schistosome egg plays a central role in disease pathogenesis, causation and transmission.
source: The schistosome egg plays a central role in disease pathogenesis, causation and transmission (Gryseels et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The appearance of S. mansoni eggs in host tissues by 6 to 7 weeks after infection coincides with profound polarization to a granulomatous, T helper type 2 (Th2) cell phenotype.
source: The appearance of S. mansoni eggs in host tissues by 6 to 7 weeks after infection coincides with profound polarization to a granulomatous, T helper type 2 (Th2) cell phenotype (Pearce et al., 2012; Everts et al., 2012; Fairfax et al., 2012; Steinfelder et al., 2009; Everts et al., 2009; Pearce et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: More than 1000 proteins have been identified in soluble egg antigen (SEA).
source: Numerous egg proteins have been characterized, with >1000 identified in a well-studied fraction termed soluble egg antigen (SEA) (Dunne et al., 1991; Curwen et al., 2004; Ashton et al., 2001; Cass et al., 2007; Mathieson and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In viable eggs, about 30 of the SEA proteins are located outside the developing miracidium and encompass the complement of secreted antigens (egg-secreted proteins, ESP) that interact with host tissues to facilitate the passage of the egg from the mesenteric veins to the intestinal lumen.
source: In viable eggs, about 30 of the SEA proteins are located outside the developing miracidium and encompass the complement of secreted antigens (egg-secreted proteins, ESP) that interact with host tissues to facilitate the passage of the egg from the mesenteric veins to the intestinal lumen (Mathieson and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The T2 ribonuclease omega-1 (ω1) is the principal Th2-inducing component of ESP.
source: The T2 ribonuclease omega-1 (ω1) is the principal Th2-inducing component of ESP with its Th2-polarizing activity dependent upon both its RNase activity and glycosylation (Steinfelder et al., 2009; Everts et al., 2009; Wilbers et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The Th2-polarizing activity of ω1 is dependent upon both its RNase activity and glycosylation.
source: The T2 ribonuclease omega-1 (ω1) is the principal Th2-inducing component of ESP with its Th2-polarizing activity dependent upon both its RNase activity and glycosylation (Steinfelder et al., 2009; Everts et al., 2009; Wilbers et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The ω1 RNase is hepatotoxic.
source: This RNase is hepatotoxic (Fitzsimmons et al., 2005), and its secretion by eggs into the granuloma regulates the pattern recognition receptor signaling pathways in dendritic cells that, in turn, prime Th2 responses from CD4+ T cells (Ferguson et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Secretion of ω1 by eggs into the granuloma regulates the pattern recognition receptor signaling pathways in dendritic cells that prime Th2 responses from CD4+ T cells.
source: This RNase is hepatotoxic (Fitzsimmons et al., 2005), and its secretion by eggs into the granuloma regulates the pattern recognition receptor signaling pathways in dendritic cells that, in turn, prime Th2 responses from CD4+ T cells (Ferguson et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Secreted ω1 provokes granulomatous inflammation around eggs traversing the wall of the intestines, and trapped in hepatic sinusoids and other host organs, driving fibrosis that eventually results in hepatointestinal schistosomiasis.
source: Secreted ω1 provokes granulomatous inflammation around eggs traversing the wall of the intestines, and trapped in hepatic sinusoids and other host organs, driving fibrosis that eventually results in hepatointestinal schistosomiasis (Gryseels et al., 2006; Wynn et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Five genomic copies of ω1 were identified in the S. mansoni reference genome, version 5.
source: Five genomic copies of ω1 were identified in the S. mansoni reference genome, version 5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), although the repetitive nature of the ω1 locus on chromosome one presents a challenge for genome assembly.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the reference genome, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The repetitive nature of the ω1 locus on chromosome one presents a challenge for genome assembly.
source: Five genomic copies of ω1 were identified in the S. mansoni reference genome, version 5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), although the repetitive nature of the ω1 locus on chromosome one presents a challenge for genome assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the genomic locus.

claim: The Smp_193860 copy of ω1 includes nine exons separated by eight introns and spans 6,196 nt.
source: A single copy of ω1 selected for genome editing, Smp_193860, included nine exons separated by eight introns and spanned 6,196 nt (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from genome analysis, supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Several other copies of ω1 shared similar exon/intron structure and conserved coding sequences.
source: Several other copies shared similar exon/intron structure and conserved coding sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from genome analysis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The predicted coding sequence (CDS) of Smp_193860 encoded a ~27 kDa protein, of similar mass to the 31 kDa reported for ω1.
source: The predicted coding sequence (CDS) of Smp_193860 encoded a ~27 kDa protein, of similar mass to the 31 kDa reported for ω1 (Murare et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, compared to prior literature.

claim: The ω1 gene encodes a secreted ribonuclease of the T2 family of transferase-type endoribonucleases with conserved catalytic regions.
source: The gene encodes a secreted ribonuclease of the T2 family of transferase-type endoribonucleases with conserved catalytic regions (Luhtala and Parker, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A sgRNA was designed targeting residues 3,808 to 3,827 of Smp_193860 within exon 6, adjacent to an AGG protospacer adjacent motif (PAM).
source: We designed a sgRNA targeting residues 3,808 to 3,827 of Smp_193860 within exon 6, adjacent to an AGG protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) and with the predicted Cas9 cleavage site located at three residues upstream of the PAM.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: The predicted Cas9 cleavage site was located at three residues upstream of the PAM.
source: We designed a sgRNA targeting residues 3,808 to 3,827 of Smp_193860 within exon 6, adjacent to an AGG protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) and with the predicted Cas9 cleavage site located at three residues upstream of the PAM.
evidence: This describes the expected behavior of Cas9 based on established knowledge.

claim: The AGG and the nucleotide sequence complementary to the sgRNA were also present in the Smp_179960 and Smp_184360 copies of ω1.
source: The AGG and the nucleotide sequence complementary to this sgRNA were also present in the Smp_179960 and Smp_184360 copies of ω1.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: The three copies of ω1 (Smp_193860, Smp_179960, and Smp_184360) shared >99% identity in the 202 bp PCR amplicon region subjected to next generation sequencing.
source: These three copies shared >99% identity in the 202 bp PCR amplicon region subjected to next generation sequencing (NGS) although they differed by several substitutions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B and C.

claim: The three copies of ω1 (Smp_193860, Smp_179960, and Smp_184360) differed by several substitutions in the 202 bp PCR amplicon region.
source: These three copies shared >99% identity in the 202 bp PCR amplicon region subjected to next generation sequencing (NGS) although they differed by several substitutions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B and C.

claim: All three copies of ω1 (Smp_193860, Smp_179960, and Smp_184360) display a tight profile of developmental stage expression: expression is restricted to the mature egg with expression not apparent elsewhere during the developmental cycle of this schistosome.
source: All three copies of ω1 display a tight profile of developmental stage expression: expression is restricted to the mature egg with expression not apparent elsewhere during the developmental cycle of this schistosome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) (Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from expression analysis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and a citation.

claim: Candidate homologues for six of seven human NHEJ pathway genes were identified in S. mansoni by searching for matches to Pfam.
source: Candidate homologues for six of seven human NHEJ pathway genes and for two key HDR pathway genes were identified by searching for matches to Pfam (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Candidate homologues for two key HDR pathway genes were identified in S. mansoni by searching for matches to Pfam.
source: Candidate homologues for six of seven human NHEJ pathway genes and for two key HDR pathway genes were identified by searching for matches to Pfam (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatic analysis.

claim: A putative homologue of Cernunnos/XLF was not apparent in S. mansoni based on searching for the Pfam XLF domain (PF09302) found in human Cernunnos/XLF.
source: A putative homologue of Cernunnos/XLF was not apparent in S. mansoni (Deriano and Roth, 2013) based on searching for the Pfam XLF domain (PF09302) found in human Cernunnos/XLF.
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The XLF domain appears to be absent from all flatworm species studied by the International Helminth Genomes Consortium.
source: The domain appears to be absent from all flatworm species studied by the International Helminth Genomes Consortium (International Helminth Genomes Consortium, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A ribonucleoprotein complex (RNP) comprising of sgRNA mixed with recombinant Cas9 endonuclease was delivered into schistosome eggs isolated from livers of experimentally infected mice by electroporation.
source: First, a ribonucleoprotein complex (RNP) comprising of sgRNA mixed with recombinant Cas9 endonuclease was delivered into schistosome eggs isolated from livers of experimentally infected mice (eggs termed 'LE', for 'liver eggs') by electroporation.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The ssODN included a short transgene encoding six stop codons flanked by 5'- and 3'-homology arms, each arm 50 nt in length, complementary to the genome sequence of exon 6 on the 5´ and 3´ sides of the Cas9 cleavage site.
source: The ssODN included a short transgene encoding six stop codons flanked by 5'- and 3'-homology arms, each arm 50 nt in length, complementary to the genome sequence of exon 6 on the 5´ and 3´ sides of the Cas9 cleavage site (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design, supported by Figure 1A and B.

claim: A lentivirus vector (pLV-ω1X6) that included Cas9, driven by the mammalian translational elongation factor one promoter, and the exon 6-targeting sgRNA (20 nt), driven by the human U6 promoter was engineered.
source: In a second approach, a lentivirus vector (pLV-ω1X6; Figure 1A and B) that included Cas9, driven by the mammalian translational elongation factor one promoter, and the exon 6-targeting sgRNA (20 nt), driven by the human U6 promoter (Duvoisin et al., 2012) was engineered.
evidence: This describes the experimental design, supported by Figure 1A and B and a citation.

claim: LE were transduced with pseudotyped lentiviral virions (pLV) by exposure in culture to LE for 24 hr.
source: LE were transduced with pseudotyped lentiviral virions (pLV) by exposure in culture to LE for 24 hr (Rinaldi et al., 2012a; Suttiprapa et al., 2016) and, thereafter, transfected with the ssODN repair template.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study, supported by citations.

claim: Amplicons of the expected sizes of 184, 285 and 321 nt were observed in genome-edited eggs but not in control eggs, a diagnostic pattern indicative of the ssODN transgene insertion into ω1.
source: Amplicons of the expected sizes of 184, 285 and 321 nt were observed in genome-edited eggs but not in control eggs (Figure 1A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), a diagnostic pattern indicative of the ssODN transgene insertion into ω1 and, in turn, indicating that the resolution of the DSB at the ω1 locus from CRISPR/Cas9 had been mediated by HDR.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by PCR data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The resolution of the DSB at the ω1 locus from CRISPR/Cas9 had been mediated by HDR.
source: Amplicons of the expected sizes of 184, 285 and 321 nt were observed in genome-edited eggs but not in control eggs (Figure 1A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), a diagnostic pattern indicative of the ssODN transgene insertion into ω1 and, in turn, indicating that the resolution of the DSB at the ω1 locus from CRISPR/Cas9 had been mediated by HDR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCR results showing transgene insertion.

claim: Sanger sequence analysis of the knocked-in amplicons (KI-R1, KI-R2 and KI-R3) confirmed the presence of the transgene inserted into ω1 at the site targeted for programmed cleavage.
source: Sanger sequence analysis of the knocked-in amplicons (KI-R1, KI-R2 and KI-R3) confirmed the presence of the transgene inserted into ω1 at the site targeted for programmed cleavage (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by sequencing data, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: More than 56 million sequenced reads were compared to the reference amplicon sequence of the Smp_193860 locus.
source: More than 56 million sequenced reads were compared to the reference amplicon sequence of the Smp_193860 locus (Supplementary file 3), which revealed that 71% exhibited the wild type (WT; i.e., unmodified DNA) whereas 29% reads exhibited apparent mutations (Figure 2D) across the 202 bp amplicon, with 0.13% insertions, 0.58% deletions and 28.2% substitutions (Supplementary file 3, sample 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding from NGS analysis.

claim: 71% of sequenced reads exhibited the wild type (WT; i.e., unmodified DNA) whereas 29% reads exhibited apparent mutations across the 202 bp amplicon in the CRISPR/Cas9-treated sample.
source: More than 56 million sequenced reads were compared to the reference amplicon sequence of the Smp_193860 locus (Supplementary file 3), which revealed that 71% exhibited the wild type (WT; i.e., unmodified DNA) whereas 29% reads exhibited apparent mutations (Figure 2D) across the 202 bp amplicon, with 0.13% insertions, 0.58% deletions and 28.2% substitutions (Supplementary file 3, sample 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding from NGS analysis, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the CRISPR/Cas9-treated sample, 0.13% of reads showed insertions, 0.58% showed deletions and 28.2% showed substitutions.
source: More than 56 million sequenced reads were compared to the reference amplicon sequence of the Smp_193860 locus (Supplementary file 3), which revealed that 71% exhibited the wild type (WT; i.e., unmodified DNA) whereas 29% reads exhibited apparent mutations (Figure 2D) across the 202 bp amplicon, with 0.13% insertions, 0.58% deletions and 28.2% substitutions (Supplementary file 3, sample 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding from NGS analysis.

claim: In the control eggs-only group, 76% were WT, and 24% of reads exhibited apparent mutations, with 0.14% insertions, 0.33% deletions, and 24.0% substitutions.
source: In contrast, in the control eggs-only group, 76% were WT, and 24% of reads exhibited apparent mutations, with 0.14% insertions, 0.33% deletions, and 24.0% substitutions (Figure 2E, sample two in Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from NGS analysis, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Subtracting the rate of apparent mutations in the control, 0.25% and 4.2% of reads in the experimental sample carried programmed CRISPR-induced deletions and substitutions, respectively.
source: Thus, subtracting the rate of apparent mutations in the control, we estimated that 0.25% and 4.2% of reads in the experimental sample carried programmed CRISPR-induced deletions and substitutions, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the NGS data comparing experimental and control samples.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas9-treated sample displayed a higher rate of frame-shifts compared to a sample from control eggs, 2.0% versus 1.4%.
source: Indels of 1–2 bp, or multiples thereof, in coding DNA cause frame-shifts, and consistent with its higher rate of indels, the CRISPR/Cas9-treated sample displayed a higher rate of frame-shifts compared to a sample from control eggs, 2.0% versus 1.4%).
evidence: This is a primary finding from NGS analysis.

claim: Many apparent sequence variants common to the control and edited eggs likely reflect polymorphism among copies of ω1 rather than programmed mutations.
source: Many apparent sequence variants common to the control and edited eggs likely reflect polymorphism among copies of ω1 rather than programmed mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of common variants in both control and experimental samples.

claim: Insertion of the 24 bp transgene was confirmed in 0.19% of the reads at the sgRNA programmed CRISPR/Cas9 target site.
source: Here, insertion of the 24 bp transgene was confirmed in 0.19% of the reads at the sgRNA programmed CRISPR/Cas9 target site (Figure 2F, sample nine in Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from NGS analysis, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Some reads containing the knock-in sequence included the 'CC' to 'TA' substitutions at positions 152–153 and 'AC' to 'TT' at positions 60–61.
source: Some reads containing the knock-in sequence included the 'CC' to 'TA' substitutions at positions 152–153 and 'AC' to 'TT' at positions 60–61 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from NGS analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The indels catalyzed by NHEJ and/or KI by HDR occurred in target DNA sequences which exhibited 99% identity in multiple copies of ω1 including Smp_193860, Smp_184360 and Smp_179960.
source: This indicates that the indels catalyzed by NHEJ and/or KI by HDR occurred in target DNA sequences which exhibited 99% identity in multiple copies of ω1 including Smp_193860, Smp_184360 and Smp_179960, and possibly also further copies not yet annotated in the reference genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence similarity among ω1 copies and the mutation patterns observed.

claim: The qPCR approach estimated a reduction by 12.5% in relative fold amplification in the pLV-ω1X6 with ssODN treatment group.
source: The qPCR approach estimated a reduction by 12.5% in relative fold amplification in the pLV-ω1X6 with ssODN treatment group (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), whereas CRISPResso analysis of the pooled NGS reads indicated a frequency of indel/substitution mutation of ~4.5% (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from qPCR analysis, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CRISPResso analysis of the pooled NGS reads indicated a frequency of indel/substitution mutation of ~4.5%.
source: The qPCR approach estimated a reduction by 12.5% in relative fold amplification in the pLV-ω1X6 with ssODN treatment group (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), whereas CRISPResso analysis of the pooled NGS reads indicated a frequency of indel/substitution mutation of ~4.5% (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from NGS analysis.

claim: Liver eggs (LE) transfected with RNP complexes, with or without ssODN, displayed a downregulation of the ω1-specific transcript of ~45% and 81%, respectively, compared to controls.
source: Liver eggs (LE) transfected with RNP complexes, with or without ssODN, displayed a downregulation of the ω1-specific transcript of ~45% and 81%, respectively, compared to controls (p≤0.05; n = 11 by one way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a primary finding from transcript analysis with statistical support.

claim: LE transduced with pLV-ω1X6 virions, with or without ssODN, showed a reduction of the ω1-specific transcripts of 67% and 83% respectively, when compared to controls.
source: However, LE transduced with pLV-ω1X6 virions, with or without ssODN, showed a reduction of the ω1-specific transcripts of 67% and 83% respectively, when compared to controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from transcript analysis, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Resolution of chromosomal DSB by NHEJ plus HDR provided enhanced programmed gene knockout compared to NHEJ-mediated chromosomal repair alone.
source: This outcome indicated that resolution of chromosomal DSB by NHEJ plus HDR provided enhanced programmed gene knockout compared to NHEJ-mediated chromosomal repair alone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of transcript reduction with and without ssODN.

claim: Both RNPs and pLV virions efficiently delivered programmed gene editing to schistosomes but lentiviral transduction delivered enhanced performance with stronger gene silencing, in particular when the donor repair template was provided.
source: Nevertheless, both RNPs and pLV virions efficiently delivered programmed gene editing to schistosomes but lentiviral transduction delivered enhanced performance with stronger gene silencing, in particular when the donor repair template was provided (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of experimental results, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When examined at later time points (days 5 and 7 following manipulation of the LE), further reduction in ω1 abundance was not apparent.
source: When examined at later time points (days 5 and 7 following manipulation of the LE), further reduction in ω1 abundance was not apparent (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course transcript analysis, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Wild type SEA exhibited marked RNase activity against the yeast RNA; ~70 ng RNA remained intact after one hour, corresponding to >60% digestion.
source: Wild type SEA exhibited marked RNase activity against the yeast RNA;~70 ng RNA remained intact after one hour, corresponding to >60% digestion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNase activity assay.

claim: Incubation of the RNA with Δω1-SEA from the experimental groups resulted in ~30% substrate digestion.
source: Incubation of the RNA with Δω1-SEA (i.e. SEA from the gene edited eggs) from the experimental groups, RNP, RNP +ssODN, pLV-ω1X6, and pLV-ω1X6 + ssODN, resulted in ~30% substrate digestion, with 124, 140, 135 and 153 ng of RNA remaining, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNase activity assay.

claim: All conditions for programmed genome editing resulted in less digestion of the yeast RNA than for wild type SEA (p≤0.0001).
source: All conditions for programmed genome editing resulted in less digestion of the yeast RNA than for wild type SEA (p≤0.0001) (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNase activity assay with statistical support, shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The Δω1-SEA with programmed knock-in exhibited less RNase activity than Δω1-SEA prepared without the donor ssODN repair template (p≤0.01, n = 6 by one-way ANOVA).
source: Moreover, the Δω1-SEA with programmed knock-in exhibited less RNase activity than Δω1-SEA prepared without the donor ssODN repair template (p≤0.01, n = 6 by one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNase activity assay with statistical support.

claim: Ribonuclease ω1 alone is capable of conditioning human monocyte-derived dendritic cells to drive Th2 polarization.
source: The ω1 ribonuclease alone is capable of conditioning human monocyte-derived dendritic cells to drive Th2 polarization (Everts et al., 2012) and enhanced CD11b+ macrophage modulation of intracellular toll like receptor (TLR) signaling (Ferguson et al., 2015; Ferguson et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ribonuclease ω1 enhances CD11b+ macrophage modulation of intracellular toll like receptor (TLR) signaling.
source: The ω1 ribonuclease alone is capable of conditioning human monocyte-derived dendritic cells to drive Th2 polarization (Everts et al., 2012) and enhanced CD11b+ macrophage modulation of intracellular toll like receptor (TLR) signaling (Ferguson et al., 2015; Ferguson et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ribonuclease ω1 inhibited TLR-induced production of IL-1β and redirected the TLR signaling outcome toward an anti-inflammatory profile via the mannose receptor (MR) and dectin.
source: Ribonuclease ω1 inhibited TLR-induced production of IL-1β and redirected the TLR signaling outcome toward an anti-inflammatory profile via the mannose receptor (MR) and dectin (Everts et al., 2012; Zaccone et al., 2011; Ritter et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SEA from ω1-mutated eggs reduced levels of Th2 cytokines, including IL-4 and IL-5, in comparison to wild-type SEA (p≤0.01).
source: SEA from ω1-mutated eggs reduced levels of Th2 cytokines, including IL-4 and IL-5, in comparison to wild-type SEA (p≤0.01), and a trend toward less IL-13 production was also observed (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the co-culture assay with statistical support, shown in Figure 4.

claim: A trend toward less IL-13 production was observed in co-cultures exposed to SEA from ω1-mutated eggs.
source: SEA from ω1-mutated eggs reduced levels of Th2 cytokines, including IL-4 and IL-5, in comparison to wild-type SEA (p≤0.01), and a trend toward less IL-13 production was also observed (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the co-culture assay, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Reduced levels of IL-6 and TNF-α were observed in co-cultures exposed to SEA from ω1-mutated eggs (p≤0.01, n = 4 by one-way ANOVA).
source: Reduced levels of IL-6 and TNF-α were also observed (p≤0.01, n = 4 by one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the co-culture assay with statistical support.

claim: Significant differences in IL-10 and IL-2 were not evident between the WT- and mutant-SEA groups.
source: By contrast, significant differences in IL-10 and IL-2 were not evident between the WT- and mutant-SEA groups.
evidence: This is a finding from the co-culture assay.

claim: IFN-γ was not detected following pulsing with the WT-SEA or mutant-SEA.
source: IFN-γ was not detected following pulsing with the WT-SEA or mutant-SEA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
